Njẹ́ àyẹ̀wò kan wà tí a lè ṣe, tí a lè fi mọ ohun pàtó tí ó fa irúfẹ́ nǹkan wọ̀nyí? Àbí dídúró níbi tí erùkù wà rẹ̀ ni ó fa èyí ni tàbí àgọ́ ara rẹ̀ ni ó ń yí padà tí irú èyí fi ń ṣẹlẹ̀? Irú òògùn wo ni ó lè lò tí mímí rẹ̀ yóò fi máa já gẹ́rẹ́gẹ́ ní gbogbo ìgbà àti ní òrékóre, ní ibikíbi tí ó bá wà?
model_answer:
Your husband’s symptoms are most suggestive of asthma or allergic airway disease, triggered by dust, smoke, frying fumes, and strong smells, but he should be examined to rule out infections such as tuberculosis, especially if cough lasts over 2 weeks, or there is fever, weight loss, night sweats, or blood in sputum.  
He should visit a clinic for chest examination, oxygen level, peak-flow/spirometry if available, and possibly chest X-ray or sputum test depending on findings.  
Meanwhile, reduce triggers: keep rooms well ventilated, avoid smoke/perfumes/frying fumes, clean dust with a wet cloth, use a face mask in dusty places, and avoid indoor charcoal/firewood smoke.  
For quick relief of wheezing or tight breathing, a salbutamol inhaler can help, but frequent symptoms usually need a doctor-prescribed preventer inhaler such as inhaled corticosteroid; sneezing/runny nose may improve with cetirizine or loratadine and a steroid nasal spray.  
If he has severe breathlessness, cannot speak full sentences, lips turn bluish, chest pain, confusion, or salbutamol is not helping, take him to emergency care immediately.

question: Ìyá ọmọ kan tó ń gbé ní ilé wa ló lóyún ọmọ rẹ̀ kejì bẹ̀rẹ̀ oyún náà gbogbo nǹkan lọ déédéé inú rẹ̀ sí dùn pé ọmọ tuntun ń bọ̀ ṣùgbọ́n ní oṣù díẹ̀ sẹ́yìn ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní ìrora tó lágbára ní ìsàlẹ̀ inú ọjọ́ kan ìrora náà pọ̀ tó bẹ́ẹ̀ tí kò lè fi dìde dáadáa kò pé o tún bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní Rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ púpọ̀ tó ń lára rẹ̀ náà ju bí ẹ̀jẹ̀ yìí pọ̀ ju bó máa rí lọ ó sì máa mọ̀kó rẹ̀ gan-anbá bóyá ọmọ inú rẹ̀ wà nínú ewu ní kíákíá ni ọkọ rẹ̀ lọ́wọ́ láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn ìbéèrè mi ni ó lè fa ìrora? tó lágbára ní ìsàlẹ̀ inú nígbà oyún ṣé ẹ̀jẹ̀ púpọ̀ tó ń yọ nígbà oyún jẹ́ àmì ewu fún ìyá tàbí ọmọ inú rẹ̀ kí ni àwọn àfihàn tó fi hàn pé oyún náà wà nínú ìṣòro wà tó lè dá ìrora àti ẹ̀jẹ̀ dúró láì bá ọmọ inú rẹ̀ jẹ́?
reference:
Ìyá ọmọ kan tó ń gbé ní ẹ̀gbẹ́ ilé wa ni ó lóyún ọmọ rẹ̀ kejì. Ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀ oyún náà, gbogbo nǹkan ń lọ dédé, inú rẹ̀ sì dùn pé, ọmọ tuntun ń bọ̀. Ṣùgbọ́n ní oṣù díẹ̀ sẹ́yìn, ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní ní ìrora tó lágbára ní ìsàlẹ̀ inú. Ní ọjọ́ kan, ìrora náà pọ̀ tó bẹ́ẹ̀ tí kò lè fi dìde dáadáa. Kò pé, ó tún bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ púpọ̀, tó ń yọ lára rẹ̀. Ẹ̀jẹ̀ náà ju bíi. Ẹ̀jẹ̀ yìí pọ̀ ju bí ó ṣe máa ń rí lọ, ó sì máa ń mú kó rẹ̀ gan. Bí ó ṣe rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ yìí, ẹ̀rù bà á pé bóyá ọmọ inú rẹ̀ wà nínú ewu. Ní kíákíá ni ọkọ rẹ̀ ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn.
Ìbéèrè mi ni kí ni ó lè fa ìrora tó lágbára ní ìsàlẹ̀ inú nígbà oyún? Ṣé ẹ̀jẹ̀ púpọ̀ tó ń yọ nígbà oyún jẹ́ àmì ewu fún ìyá tàbí ọmọ inú rẹ̀?
Kí ni àwọn àfihàn tó fi hàn pé oyún náà wà nínú ìṣòro? Ṣé òògùn wà tó lè da ìrora àti ẹ̀jẹ̀ dúró, láì ba ọmọ inú rẹ̀ jẹ?
model_answer:
Severe lower abdominal pain with heavy bleeding in pregnancy is a danger sign for both mother and baby and needs emergency care immediately.  
Possible causes include miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption, placenta previa, preterm labour, infection, or rarely uterine rupture, depending on the pregnancy age.  
Warning signs that the pregnancy is in trouble include heavy bleeding or clots, severe or persistent pain, dizziness/fainting, fever, reduced or absent baby movements, leaking fluid, or contractions before term.  
At the hospital, doctors will check her blood pressure and pulse, examine her, do an ultrasound and fetal heartbeat check, blood tests, and give IV fluids, safe pain relief, medicines, blood transfusion, or surgery/early delivery if needed.  
She should not take herbs, insert anything into the vagina, or wait at home; prompt treatment is the safest way to protect both mother and baby.

A 5‑month‑old baby with cough and any breathing difficulty should be taken to a health centre or hospital today, because this can be pneumonia or bronchiolitis and may need oxygen, nebulization, or antibiotics after examination.  
Go urgently if breathing is fast (>50 breaths/min), the chest is pulling in, the baby cannot breastfeed, is very weak/sleepy, has fever, vomiting, convulsions, or bluish lips.  
Do not give cough mixtures, antibiotics, herbal mixtures, menthol/camphor rubs, or honey, as these can be harmful at this age.  
At home while going for care, clear the nose with normal saline drops and gentle suction, keep the baby upright, continue frequent breastfeeding/expressed breast milk, and avoid smoke, dust, and cold exposure.  
Since the baby is only 5 months, try to return to exclusive breast milk until 6 months if possible, or leave expressed breast milk with the grandmother.

This is primary postpartum haemorrhage, most commonly from uterine atony, but also consider retained placental tissue, genital tract tears, uterine rupture/inversion, or a bleeding disorder.  
Treat immediately: call for help, monitor vital signs, start two large-bore IV lines, give crystalloids, crossmatch/arrange blood, empty the bladder, massage the uterus, and examine the placenta, cervix, vagina and perineum for retained tissue or tears.  
Give uterotonics urgently: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV then infusion if available; if bleeding continues add misoprostol 800–1000 micrograms rectally or sublingually, and ergometrine 0.2 mg IM/IV only if no hypertension; give tranexamic acid 1 g IV as soon as possible, repeat once after 30 minutes if ongoing bleeding.  
If retained placenta/tissue is suspected, perform manual removal/evacuation with analgesia and antibiotics; repair tears, and use bimanual uterine compression or condom/balloon tamponade if atony persists.  
She should be referred urgently to a higher-level hospital if bleeding is heavy or not rapidly controlled, but resuscitation and the above life-saving measures must start before and during transfer.

This woman should be treated as having postpartum haemorrhage or acute anaemia until proven otherwise, even if the bleeding is not obvious.  
Immediately check her pulse, blood pressure, pallor, level of consciousness, uterine tone, vaginal bleeding, placenta completeness, and look for cervical/vaginal tears or retained products.  
Call for help, start two wide-bore IV lines, give crystalloids, take blood for PCV/Hb, grouping and crossmatch, and prepare urgent blood transfusion if she is shocked, very pale, or Hb/PCV is low.  
Massage the uterus and give uterotonics such as oxytocin; if oxytocin is unavailable, use misoprostol according to protocol, while treating the cause: uterine atony, retained placenta/products, or genital tract tear.

Ní àárọ̀ ọjọ́ kejì, ó rí pé ọmọ náà kò fẹ́ mú ọmú tàbí ṣeré bí ti tẹ́lẹ̀, ìyá náà sì pinnu láti lọ bá dókítà nítorí ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa ikọ́ àti ìṣòro bí ó ṣe ń mí kí ó lè mọ ohun tó máa lò fún ọmọ náà. Ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ kékeré máa wọ́ ikọ́ gan ní alẹ́ tí ó dè tún ṣòro fún láti máa mí dáadáa? Ṣé ikọ́ àti bí ó ṣe ń tiraka láti mí dáadáa lè jẹ́ àmì àìsàn èdò-foró? Kí ni àwọn nkan tí wọ́n lè ṣe ní ilé láti lè jẹ́ kí ọmọ náà kò tìbọ̀ lè rọrùn sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́?
model_answer:
Night cough with breathing difficulty in an 8‑month‑old can be due to viral bronchiolitis/common cold, pneumonia, wheezing/asthma-like illness, croup, or less commonly whooping cough or reflux.  
Yes, fast breathing, chest indrawing, noisy breathing, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, or inability to play can be signs of pneumonia or severe chest infection and the child should be seen urgently today; for 2–12 months, breathing rate of 50/minute or more is concerning.  
At home while going to hospital, keep the baby sitting slightly upright, continue breastfeeding in small frequent feeds, clear the nose with saline drops and gentle suction, and keep the room free of smoke, dust, kerosene fumes, and strong perfumes.  
Do not give cough syrups, antibiotics without prescription, or honey because the child is under 1 year; paracetamol can be used only if there is fever or pain at the correct dose.  
Seek emergency care immediately if the lips look blue, breathing is very difficult, the child cannot breastfeed, becomes very weak, has convulsions, or the chest is pulling in with each breath.

question: Aláboyún kan tó lóyún oṣù mẹ́fà tó ń gbé ní ilé wa tó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ṣàkíyèsí pé ọkàn máa ń mí ẹlẹ bí ẹni pé òun ṣẹ̀ sáré tán nigbà míì ó máa ń rẹ láì ṣe iṣẹ́ kankan rẹ̀ sì máa ń gbọ̀n díẹ̀díẹ̀yìn ọ̀sẹ̀ mélòó kan ó tún rí ọrùn ẹ ti bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí. ní iwájú nígbà tí àwọn ènìyàn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń sọ pé orun rẹ̀ yàtọ̀ sí ti tẹ́lẹ̀ ó bẹ̀rù gan àwọn àìsàn tó máa ń ṣe aláboyún ni àbí ìṣòro mìíràn ó dẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ orí dókítà kí wọ́n ba lè mọ irú nǹkan tó fa ni pé kí ni ó lè fàá kí ọkàn aláboyún kó máa dà wípé wọn. Omi ẹ̀lẹ́bẹ̀ ẹni tó ṣẹ̀ṣẹ̀ sáré tán pẹ̀lú kí ọrùn rẹ̀ máa wú ìṣòro yìí lè ní ipa lórí ìdàgbàsókè onnú ẹní àwọn àmì ewu tí ó jẹ́ kí wọ́n yàra fún ní inú ilé àwọn oúnjẹ kan wà bí ohun mímu kan wà tí ó yẹ kí ó yàgò fún tàbí elé tó yẹ kó máa jẹ? Pọ si ní àsìkò yìí.
reference: Alábóyún kan tó lọ́yún oṣù mẹ́fà tọ́ ń gbé ní ilé wa, ló bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ṣàkíyèsí pé ọkàn òun máa ń mì ẹlẹ́-ẹlẹ́ bí ẹni pé òun ṣẹ̀ṣẹ̀ sáré tán ni, nígbà míràn ó máa ń rẹ̀ ẹ́ láìṣe iṣẹ́ kankan, ọwọ́ rẹ̀ sì máa ń gbọ̀n díẹ̀díẹ̀. Lẹ́yìn ọ̀sẹ̀ mélòó kan, ó tún rí i pé ọrùn rẹ̀ ti bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í wú ní iwájú. Nígbà tí àwọn ènìyàn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í sọ pé ọrùn rẹ̀ yàtọ̀ sí ti tẹ́lẹ̀, ó bẹ̀ru gan-an, ó wò pé ṣé àwọn àìsàn tó máa ń ṣe alábóyún ni àbí ìṣòro míràn? Ó dẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ rí dókítà kí wọ́n bá a lè mọ irú nǹkan tí ó ń fà á. Ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fà á kí ọkàn alábóyún kó máa dàbí pé ó ń mì ẹlẹ́-ẹlẹ́ bí ẹni tọ́ ṣẹ̀ṣẹ̀ sáré tán pẹ̀lú kí ọrùn rẹ̀ máa wú? Ṣé ìṣòro yìí lè ní ipa pẹ̀lú ìdàgbàsókè ọmọ inú rẹ̀? Kí ni àwọn àmì tí yóò yẹ  kí wọ́n yẹra fún  ní inú ilé? Ṣé àwọn óńjẹ kan wà àbí ohun mímú kan wà tí ó tọ́ kọ́ yàgò fún, àbí èleyí tí ó yẹ kọ́ máa jẹ púpọ̀ sí i níru àsìkò yìí?
model_answer:
Her symptoms suggest an overactive thyroid gland in pregnancy, often Graves’ disease, especially with palpitations, tremor, tiredness and swelling in the front of the neck; she needs urgent antenatal review with tests such as TSH, free T4/T3, blood count and blood pressure check.  
If untreated, hyperthyroidism can affect mother and baby, causing severe maternal fast heartbeat/heart failure, high blood pressure in pregnancy, miscarriage, premature birth, poor fetal growth, low birth weight, or fetal/newborn thyroid problems.  
She should go to hospital immediately if she has chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, fever with confusion/agitation, persistent very fast heartbeat, severe vomiting/dehydration, vaginal bleeding, severe headache/blurred vision, or reduced baby movements.  
Treatment is available and can be safe in pregnancy, but must be prescribed by a doctor; medicines such as antithyroid drugs may be needed and doses must be monitored carefully.  
She should avoid self-medication, herbal mixtures, excess iodine/kelp supplements, smoking, alcohol and too much caffeine, but continue normal iodized salt in moderation and eat balanced meals rich in protein, fruits/vegetables, calcium, iron and folic acid as advised in antenatal care.

Ó ní, òun wá pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, kí wọn lè mọ̀ ohun tí ó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí Pẹ́jú. Ǹjẹ́ ìṣòro yìí, lè wọ̀ fún ọmọ yìí? Ṣé àrùn àyà ni, tábí àrùn ikọ́fẹ́, ni ó lè jẹ́ fún ọmọ náà? Kí ni àwọn ohun tí ọmọ náà ní láti yàgò fún, kí ìṣòro tí ó ń ṣe e tí ó ń jẹ́ kọ́ wúkọ́ yìí kò lè dínkù dáadáa?
model_answer:
Yes, this can be dangerous in a 1-year-old, especially because the child is breathing with difficulty and the cough is worse at night.  
It may be pneumonia, bronchiolitis, asthma-like wheeze, or another chest infection; tuberculosis is less likely if it has only been a few days, but should be considered if cough lasts more than 2 weeks, with weight loss, fever, night sweats, or TB contact.  
Take the child to hospital urgently, especially if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, inability to feed, bluish lips, high fever, convulsions, or unusual sleepiness.  
Avoid herbal mixtures, smoke, dust, kerosene fumes, cold air, and giving cough medicines or antibiotics without a clinician’s prescription.  
At the hospital, the child may need oxygen level check, chest examination, malaria/other infection assessment, and treatment such as nebulization, antibiotics, or oxygen depending on the cause.

Ẹ kúùkálẹ̀ dókítà, ẹ jọ̀wọ́ o, ọmọ mi ni mo mú wá sí ilé ìwòsàn, nítorí pé mo ṣàkíyèsí pé bí ó ṣe ń mí, ọmọ náà ń dún bí ẹni pé afẹ́fẹ́ ń kọjá níbi ihò kékeré. Bẹ́ẹ̀ ni ó sì ń dún nítí. Ó sì ń dún bí ìgbà tí wọ́n bá ń fọn fèrè. Tí ó sì ń tìraka láti mí dáradára.
Tí mo sì ṣàkíyèsí pé láti bíi ọjọ́ mẹ́ta báyìí, ní alẹ́ ó máa ń kọ́ú sí. Nígbà míràn, mo máa ń rí i pé àyà rẹ̀ ń wọ̀nú, àti jáde gangan bí ẹni pé ó ń ṣiṣẹ́ takuntakun láti mí. Míì ní tí mo sì ti mú lọ sí ọ̀dọ̀ àwọn onílọ́tàá já ògùn ní àdúgbò, tí wọ́n sì bá mi fún ní ògùn iwọ́kọ̀, nítorí pé ó ń ṣe bí ẹni n kọ́ú díẹ̀díẹ̀, ṣùgbọ́n tí kọ́ú yẹn kò pọ̀. Ṣùgbọ́n pẹ̀lú gbogbo ògùn tí ó lò yìí, mo ṣàkíyèsí pé kò síṣẹ́. Bákannáà ni mímí rẹ̀ sì rí, tí kò sì lè jẹun dáradára. Ẹ jọ̀wọ́, irúfẹ́ nǹkan wo ni ó mú ọmọ mi pẹ̀lú ohun mímí fífọn báyìí? Àti pé ṣé ó ní dí àyẹ̀wò ìgbàdáyà láti lè mọ irú nǹkan tí ó ń dùn, àti bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń gùlè-gùlè? Irú àwọn ìtọ́jú wo ni mo lè fún fún ọmọ yìí láti ràn lọ́wọ́ pẹ̀lú mímí rẹ̀ láti mí dáradára ní inú ilé? Ǹjẹ́ ó ní àwọn ohun ògùn àbí ohun ìkan míràn tí mo tún lè ṣe fún ọmọ yìí?
model_answer:
Your child has danger signs: noisy wheezing breathing, chest indrawing, struggling to breathe, worse at night, and inability to feed well—this could be severe bronchiolitis, asthma/reactive airway disease, or pneumonia, and needs urgent hospital care now.  
At the hospital we should check oxygen level with a pulse oximeter, respiratory rate, temperature, chest examination, and sometimes do a chest X-ray or blood tests if pneumonia or severe infection is suspected.  
Treatment may include oxygen, nebulized salbutamol if there is wheeze/airway tightening, suctioning of blocked nose, fluids if not feeding, and antibiotics only if bacterial pneumonia is likely.  
At home while coming to hospital, keep the child sitting slightly upright, clear the nose with saline drops, give small frequent breastfeeds/fluids if able, and avoid smoke, dust, kerosene fumes, and strong smells.  
Do not continue unknown medicines from chemists or cough mixtures, and if the lips turn blue, the child becomes very weak/drowsy, breathing becomes faster, or feeding stops completely, go to emergency immediately.

Ó béèrè sọ́jú sọ́jú pé ǹjẹ́ ó ṣeé ṣe kí dókítà ó kùn ún ní ilé ọmọ rẹ̀ tí wọn ò kọ́ tọ́, tí ó ń fà á tí ẹ̀jẹ̀ rẹ̀ fi ń pọ̀? Ó tún béèrè sọ́jú sọ́jú pé kí dókítà kọ abẹ́rẹ́ tàbí ògùn fún àwọn tí ó lè mú kí ẹ̀jẹ̀ yìí kó dádúró, tí ọmọ yí ó sì fi mú okùn padà, a sì lè tọ́jú ọmọ rẹ̀.
model_answer: Yes, retained placental tissue or blood clots in the womb can cause heavy bleeding after delivery, and fever with foul bleeding suggests possible infection as well. Her paleness, cold limbs, weakness and heavy bleeding are danger signs of severe postpartum haemorrhage with shock, so she needs emergency treatment immediately. In hospital, doctors should check her blood pressure/pulse, start IV fluids, give oxygen if needed, cross-match blood and transfuse if anaemic or in shock. Medicines commonly used include oxytocin, misoprostol or ergometrine to contract the womb, plus broad-spectrum antibiotics if infection is suspected; if tissue is retained, it must be removed safely by a skilled clinician. After bleeding is controlled she will need iron/folate, nutrition and follow-up, but the priority is stopping the bleeding and treating shock/infection now.

Ní ọ̀sẹ̀ díẹ̀, ó pinnu láti lọ rí dókítà. Ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa kókó náà àti ohun tí ó yẹ kọ́ ṣe láti dábòbò ìlera rẹ̀.
Ìbérè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fa kókó líle nínú ọmú ọmọbìnrin?
Ṣé gbogbo kókó nínú ọmú ni ó túmọ̀ sí àwọn tólè wọ kánṣá?
Kí ni àwọn àmì mìíràn tí ó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún nípa ọmú náà?
model_answer:
A hard lump in a girl’s breast is often not cancer; common causes include normal breast development (“breast bud”), fibroadenoma, cyst, injury/fat necrosis, or infection/abscess, while breast cancer is very rare in children and teenagers.  
However, any lump that persists for more than 2–4 weeks, grows, is very hard or fixed, or is associated with skin dimpling, nipple pulling in, bloody nipple discharge, swollen armpit glands, fever, redness, or severe pain should be checked promptly.  
She should be taken to a doctor or breast clinic for proper examination; an ultrasound is usually the first test in young girls and is safe.  
Do not massage, squeeze, or apply herbal preparations, as this can worsen infection or delay diagnosis.  
Most lumps are benign, but early medical assessment is the best way to protect her health and give peace of mind.

This is a first-trimester bleeding emergency: likely incomplete/inevitable miscarriage, but ruptured ectopic pregnancy and molar pregnancy must be excluded because they can rapidly cause shock and death.  
Immediate management is ABC assessment, check vital signs, insert two wide-bore IV lines, give normal saline/Ringer’s lactate, send urgent blood for grouping/cross-match and transfuse if shocked or severely anaemic, while calling senior obstetric/surgical help.  
To control bleeding, give tranexamic acid 1 g IV as soon as possible if bleeding is heavy, but definitive treatment is urgent uterine evacuation by manual vacuum aspiration/suction curettage if incomplete abortion is confirmed; misoprostol may be used if stable, and give antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
If Rh-negative, give anti-D immunoglobulin; give analgesia, oxygen if unstable, and monitor urine output.  
Investigations should include urine/serum pregnancy test, pelvic examination, urgent ultrasound scan, full blood count, blood group/Rh and cross-match, clotting profile if available, and serum beta-hCG especially if ectopic pregnancy is suspected.

Yellow eyes/skin with fever, weakness, poor appetite and worsening over 3 days is a danger sign, commonly from malaria with jaundice/severe malaria in Nigeria, but also hepatitis, typhoid/sepsis, or blood destruction.  
Please take him to a hospital urgently today, especially if he is very weak, confused, vomiting repeatedly, passing dark urine, breathing fast, or not drinking.  
He should be checked with malaria test, full blood count/PCV, liver function/bilirubin, blood sugar, kidney tests, urine test, and possibly hepatitis tests.  
Treatment may include antimalarial medicine such as IV artesunate if severe, fluids, fever control, vomiting medicine, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and blood transfusion/referral if severely anaemic.  
Avoid alcohol, herbal mixtures, and excess paracetamol, as these can worsen liver injury.

This pregnant woman likely has pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure with headache, facial/hand swelling and possible visual symptoms), so she should be admitted, have urine protein checked, blood tests for platelets, kidney/liver function, and fetal assessment.  
Safe blood pressure medicines in pregnancy include labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa, and hydralazine; avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs such as enalapril, lisinopril, losartan, and avoid self-medication/herbal mixtures.  
If she has severe headache, visual symptoms, very high BP, or fits risk, give magnesium sulphate to prevent seizures and control BP urgently.  
She should rest preferably on her left side, attend antenatal care regularly, reduce excess salt, avoid alcohol/smoking, avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen/diclofenac unless prescribed, and report immediately if headache, blurred vision, severe abdominal pain, reduced fetal movement, bleeding, or fits occur.  
Definitive treatment for severe pre-eclampsia is delivery when mother or baby is at risk, with timing depending on gestational age and severity.

A baby with fast or difficult breathing and a severe cough may have pneumonia, bronchiolitis, whooping cough, asthma/wheezing illness, aspiration of milk/food, or sometimes severe malaria/anemia or heart disease; it is not usually caused simply by cold water or exposing the chest.  
This can become dangerous quickly, especially if there is chest indrawing, noisy breathing, bluish lips, poor feeding, fever, convulsions, extreme sleepiness, or breathing faster than normal for age.  
Take the child to a hospital or health centre immediately for assessment, oxygen level check, and treatment such as oxygen, antibiotics if pneumonia is likely, and nebulization if wheezing is present.  
Do not give cough mixtures, antibiotics, or herbal remedies without a clinician’s advice, and keep the baby warm, upright, and breastfeeding/feeding small amounts if able.  
Ensure immunizations are up to date, especially pentavalent, pneumococcal, measles, and pertussis-containing vaccines.

Take the 7-year-old to hospital immediately; dog bites can cause wound infection, tetanus, and rabies, and traditional applications can worsen infection.

If the dog can be found, it should be observed by a vet for 10 days, but treatment should not be delayed while waiting.

This most likely sounds like measles, especially with fever, cough, red eyes/rash, and poor feeding, but the child must be examined urgently to rule out pneumonia, malaria, sepsis, or severe allergic rash.  
Do not rely on traditional herbs or black soap, as they can irritate the skin, delay proper care, or cause poisoning.  
Take the child to a hospital/clinic now for assessment, fever control, fluids/feeding support, vitamin A, and treatment of complications; antibiotics or injections are only needed if there is a bacterial complication such as pneumonia or ear infection.  
Keep the child away from other children because measles spreads easily, and ensure vaccination for contacts who are not immunized.

question: ọmọ kan le wa to ṣẹ̀ṣẹ̀ bímọ tuntun ní ọ̀sẹ̀ méjì sẹ́yìn ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ díẹ̀díẹ̀ ní ojú ara rẹ̀ ṣùgbọ́n bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ ń ṣàkíyèsí pé nǹkan bí ìpin jáde nígbà mí àwọ̀ rẹ̀ yàtọ̀ ó sì ní oòrùn tí kò dára Ó sì ńá máa ń ní ìrora kékeré ní ìsàlẹ̀ ikùn rẹ̀ ní gbogbo ìgbà tó bá ń rí àmì wọ̀nyí ọkàn rẹ̀ máa ń dàrú ó ń ronú bóyá èyí jẹ́ nǹkan nínú àwọn ìṣòro tó wọ́pọ̀ lẹ́yìn ìbímọ tàbí ìṣòro ìmí ọjọ́ kan nígbà tó lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn tó ń bá àwọn ìyá mìíràn sọ̀rọ̀ Ó gbọ́ pé kò yẹ kí wọ́n fojú tẹmẹ́lú àyípadà kankan tí wọ́n bá rí ní ara wọn èyí mú kí ó pinnu láti rí dókítà láti bá wọn sọ̀rọ̀ ìbéèrè mi ní pé kí ni ó lè fa aró nǹkan yìí lẹ́yìn ìbímọ ìrora ní ìsàlẹ̀ i jẹ́? Kini awọn aami ewu ti iyamọ tuntun yi yẹ ki o ma ṣọra fun ibimọ kini awọn igbese imototo ti iya ọmọ naa ni lati telu lati dènà àìsàn lẹ́yìn ìbímọ?
reference: Ìyá ọmọ kan ní ìwà tó ṣe bí ọmọ tútùn, ní ọ̀sẹ̀ méjì sẹ́yìn. Ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ díẹ̀-díẹ̀ ní ojú ara rẹ̀. Ṣùgbọ́n bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ó ń sàkíyèsí pé ǹkan bí ikun àti ẹ̀jẹ̀ wá ń jáde. Nígbà mìíràn ìyá ọmọ rẹ̀ yí yàtọ̀. Ó sì ní ọrùn tí kò dára. Ó sì mọ pé ìyá ọmọ náà ma ń ní ìrora kékeré nì ìṣàlẹ̀ ikùn rẹ̀, ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá rí àmì wọ̀nyí, ọkàn rẹ̀ má ń dáru. Ó rò nù bóyá ẹ̀yì jẹ́ ǹkan nínú àwọn ìṣòro tó wọ́pọ̀ lẹ́yìn ìbímọ tàbí ìṣòro mìíràn. Ní ọjọ́ kan nígbà tó lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, tó n bá àwọn ìyá mìíràn sọ̀rọ̀, ó gbọ́ pé kò yẹ kí wọn fojú tẹ́nbẹ́lú àyípadà kankan tí wọn bá rí ní ara wọn. Èyí mú kí ó wá rí dókítà láti bá wọn sọ̀rọ̀. Ìbéèrè mí ní pè, kíní ó léè fa irú ǹkan yìí lẹ́yìn ìbímọ? Ṣé ìrora nì ìṣàlẹ̀ ikùn lè jẹ́ àmì àrùn kan? Kíní àwọn àmì wo tí ìyá ọmọ tútù yìí yẹ kí ó ma ṣọ́ra fún, lẹ́yìn ìbímọ? Kíní àwọn ìbèsèyí ìyá mọ́ tó ní láti tẹ́mọ́ láti dẹ́mọ́ àìsàn yìí?
model_answer:
This may be postpartum infection (puerperal sepsis/endometritis), especially because the discharge has a bad smell and there is lower abdominal pain; retained pieces of placenta or blood clots, infected tears/episiotomy, or poor hygiene can also cause it.  
She should go to a hospital urgently for examination, temperature check, pelvic assessment, and treatment, usually antibiotics and sometimes evacuation if retained products are present.  
Danger signs after delivery include fever or chills, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding or large clots, worsening lower abdominal pain, dizziness/fainting, severe headache/blurred vision, swollen painful leg, chest pain/shortness of breath, painful urination, or breast redness with fever.  
To prevent infection, she should wash hands before touching the genital area or baby, change maternity pads often, wash the perineum with clean water and wipe front-to-back, keep wounds clean and dry, avoid douching or inserting herbs/cloth/fingers into the vagina, and avoid sex until bleeding stops and she is medically fit.  
She should also attend postnatal clinic, take prescribed medicines fully, eat well, drink clean water, and seek care early if symptoms worsen.

question: Ọmọ mi ọmọ mi obìnrin wà nínú oyún ó ti le ní ogó ọdún ó lé merin ló wà nínú eyín àtigbà tí ó ti di ọdun ó di ọdọ mi ní ìjẹta yẹn báyìí nígbà tó máa di omí mo ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní mu ó sì ti kọ́. Mo gbogbo eru re o ti ko wa sọ mi omo yin mo ṣayin pe o n mu fi silẹ mo ba sadi gbogbo eru re pe o ja ma lo si ile-iwosan a ba samu de ile iwosan ba mi yewo wọn sọ pe ile omo ti ṣi o ti n ṣe bodie naa loku ti o fi ṣetan ti o ma di ana omo lo so di omo. bo nijẹta di ana ọmọ náà sì wà ní ibi tó ti ń rọbí láti ìjẹta ó ń rọbí ọmọ òsì bota omo alakobi si mi alakobi re si lube lo wa to ti n robi latanu omo obota egun si n ba mi aya mi n ja mi ifẹ padanu omo mi si fe padanu omo to n bo naa Lako kini nkan to fa omo naa to fi wa n ro bi to pepepe ma n se awon alakobi ni o ba fe bimo ni abi se omo naa se ose ko jẹ ki bi o ti tobi ju ti o wa le gba ibi oju ara omo mi yii ni abi se ose ko jẹ pe wọn maa se abe fun omo naa tori
reference:
Ọmọ mi obìnrin wà nínú oyún, ó ti lè jẹ́ ọmọ ọdún mẹ́rìnlélógún. Òun ni ó wà nínú oyún. Lónìí ni ìṣẹ̀lẹ̀ yìí ṣẹlẹ̀.
Nígbà tí ó di alẹ́, mo ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ní ìrora. Ó sì ti kó ẹrù rẹ̀, ó ti wá sí ilé mi. Bí ìrora ṣe ń lọ, mo rí i pé ó ń pọ̀ sí i. Mo kó gbogbo ẹrù rẹ̀ jọ, kò sì jẹ́ kí a lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀.
A gbé e dé ilé ìwòsàn, wọ́n sì ṣàyẹ̀wò rẹ̀. Wọ́n sọ pé ilé-ọmọ ti bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í ṣí díẹ̀, àti pé kù díẹ̀ ni yóò tó ìgbà ìbímọ.
Ní òní ṣáájú, ilé-ọmọ ṣi ń ṣí sí i títí dé ìgbà tí ọmọ yóò fi bọ̀. Nígbà tí ó di ana, ọmọ náà wà nínú ìrora tí ó ń túbọ̀ ń pọ̀ sí i láti ìgbà tí a dé ibẹ̀.
Ó ń ní ìrora, ọmọ yóò sì bọ̀, ọmọ àkọ́bí ni. Ẹ̀rù sì ń bà mí, ọkàn sì ń bà mí.
Mo fẹ́ gba ọmọ mi là, mi ò sì fẹ́ pàdánù ọmọ tí ń bọ̀. Ẹ jọ̀wọ́, kí ni ó lè fà ìrora yìí tí ó ń ń lọ báyìí? Ṣé bó ṣe máa ń rí fún àwọn alábọ̀bí ni yẹn nígbà tí wọ́n fẹ́ bí? Ṣé ó ṣeé ṣe kó jẹ́ pé ọmọ náà ti tóbi jù, tí kò lè jáde lọ́nà ìbímọ? Tàbí ṣé ó ṣeé ṣe kó jẹ́ pé wọ́n máa ṣe iṣẹ́ abẹ fún un?
model_answer:
This sounds like prolonged or obstructed labour, which is an emergency, especially if she has been in labour for many hours/days or her waters have broken.  
Common causes include a baby that is too big for the mother’s pelvis, poor baby position, weak contractions, or the cervix not opening well; it is more common in first pregnancies but it is not normal to “keep trying” for days.  
She needs urgent assessment in a hospital with capability for Caesarean section, blood transfusion, antibiotics, and fetal monitoring, because delay can lead to loss of the baby, heavy bleeding, infection, ruptured womb, or death of the mother.  
If the cervix is not progressing, the baby is distressed, or the baby cannot pass through the birth canal, Caesarean section is the correct and lifesaving treatment.  
Please do not manage this at home or with a traditional birth attendant—take her immediately to a proper hospital or request referral now.

question: Àgbàlagbà kan ló wá sí ilé ìwòsàn alábọ́dé Baba wa yìí sọ wípé orí fò àwọn gan tí ọran wọn sì lè tí àwọn sì rí kòkòrò kan lójijì tí ó ṣú sí àwọn ní ara àwọn wà láti béèrè nǹkan tí ó lè fa àti pé irú ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún àwọn? A lọwọ baba yìí wí pé ǹjẹ́ o rí yìí ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì ni àbí ó ń fọ́ wọn wẹrẹ wẹẹrẹ àti baba yìí sì sọ wípé bọ́wẹ́rẹ́ ni orí bẹ̀rẹ̀? Ti o si ti ni agbara gan atunwa beere lọwọ baba yii wipe njẹ ti wọn ije wọn le wo ina ti wọn ba ri ina ti o mọlẹ bayi si sọ pe rara awon ko le wo ina ti o mole nitori pe o ṣe ni o ma wọ agbari awọn lọ ti orisi tun ma bere si ni fo awọn si atiwa bẹ lọwọ baba yii wipe njẹ kokoro ti o mu wọn jẹ o nle abi o? Ṣe o po abi fẹrẹ ti baba yii si sọ wipe gbogbo ara awọn ti ko si le amọ oyun awọn nigba ni abo baba yii njẹ ni ibasepo ifarakinra pẹlu alaisan ni aipẹ yii ti bayi si sọ wipe awọn ko tilẹ lọ si ibi kankan ju ki awọn ta ọja ni iwaju ile awọn ọlọ pe awọn ko ni ifarakinra pẹlu alaisan kankan ibeere wa fun. Dókítà wà ní wípé kí ló lè fa irú àìsàn orí fífọ́ orùn líle àti tí bàbá yìí kò lè yí ọrùn tí kòkòrò sì bò wọ́n ní gbogbo ara kí ló lè fa àrùn èyí ni eléyìí ni àbí nǹkan mìíràn? péye àti wípé ògùn wo lalẹ̀ ni kí baba yìí ló kí? ayéwò wọn tó dé
reference:
Bàbá àgbàlagbà kan ni wọ́n wá sí ilé ìwòsàn alábòde wa. Bàbá yìí sọ pé orí ń fò ó gan-an, ọrùn rẹ̀ sì le, ó sì ní kokoro kan ní ojijì tí ó sú sí i ní ara. Ó wá láti béèrè ohun tí ó lè fà á àti irú ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún un.
A béèrè lọ́wọ́ bàbá yìí pé ṣé orí náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì ni tàbí pé ó ti ń fò ó díẹ̀díẹ̀. Bàbá náà sì sọ pé lójijì ni ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ ní òru, ó sì ti lágbára gan-an báyìí. A tún béèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ pé ṣé ó lè wo ìmọ́lẹ̀ dáadáa, bàbá náà sì sọ pé rárá, kò lè wo ìmọ́lẹ̀ nítorí pé ó máa ń wọ agbárí rẹ̀, tí orí náà sì tún máa ń fò ó sí i.
A tún béèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ pé kokoro tí ó ń mú un yìí, ṣé ó ń le tàbí ó pọ̀, tàbí pé ó fẹ́rẹ̀fẹ́ ni. Bàbá náà sọ pé gbogbo ara òun ni, kò sì lè mọ ibi pàtó, ṣùgbọ́n ó ń yún un.
Lẹ́yìn náà, a béèrè lọ́wọ́ bàbá náà pé ṣé ó ní ìbáṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú aláìsàn kankan láìpẹ́ yìí, bàbá náà sì sọ pé wọn kò lọ sí ibi kankan ju pé wọ́n tà ọjà ní iwájú ilé wọn. Wọ́n kò sì ní ìfarakànra pẹ̀lú aláìsàn kankan.
Ìbéèrè wa fún dókítà ni pé kí ni ó lè fà irú àìsàn orífífó àti ọrùn líle tí bàbá yìí kò lè yí ọrùn rẹ̀, tí kokoro sì bò ó ní gbogbo ara? Kí ló lè fà á? Ṣé àrùn ẹyí ni èyí tàbí nǹkan míì?
Ìbéèrè wa kejì ni pé irú àyẹ̀wò wo ni a lè ní kí bàbá yìí ṣe láti mọ ohun tí ń ṣe é ní pàtó fún ìtọ́jú tó péye, àti pé oogun wo ni a lè ní kí bàbá yìí lò kí èsì àyẹ̀wò rẹ̀ tó dé?
model_answer: This is a medical emergency most consistent with acute meningitis, possibly meningococcal meningitis/septicaemia, because of sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and a widespread rash. Do not wait for test results: admit or urgently refer, check vital signs and blood glucose, give oxygen/IV fluids if needed, and take blood culture and malaria test only if they do not delay treatment. Start ceftriaxone 2 g IV/IM every 12 hours immediately; in an elderly patient add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours if available to cover Listeria. Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, plus paracetamol for fever/pain, and avoid lumbar puncture if there is coma, seizures, focal weakness, papilloedema, or shock until stabilized. Isolate the patient and give close household contacts prophylaxis according to local protocol, such as ciprofloxacin single dose, if meningococcal disease is suspected.

question: Ìyàwó kan lori wipe oko re wupọ gan ni gbogbo aarọ nigba ji lori ibusun ikona ma n bẹrẹ lẹsẹkẹsẹ o si maa n gba akoko lati dawo duro bi ọjọ ṣe n lo o tu ri pe oko re n tiraka lati mi dada nigbamii bi o ba rin jinna diẹ tabi gun atẹgun o maa n duro. láti gba ìmí rẹ̀ padà ó tún máa rẹ́ kíákíá ní alẹ́ ọjọ́ kan lẹ́yìn tí ọkọ rẹ̀ lo ìgbà pípẹ́ láti wúkọ́ àti láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà inú ìyàwó náà bàjẹ́ ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ronú bóyá àrùn kan wà lẹ́ tí ó ń fa gbogbo àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí. Ní ọjọ́ kejì ó bá ọkọ rẹ̀ sọ̀rọ̀ láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láti rí dókítà kí wọ́n lè mọ ohun tó ṣẹlẹ̀ gangan ìbéèrè ni pé kí ni ó lè fà kí ikọ́ kò lágbára tó eléyìí ní gbogbo àrà àárọ̀ dẹ́ẹ̀ tún ní ìṣòro láti mi dáadáa ní gbogbo ìgbà tó bá wuko yìí lè níse pẹ̀lú? Àrùn ẹ̀dọ̀fóró tàbí àrùn aya nìkan ni àwọn ohun tó lè mú iko àti kí máa tiraka láti mí burú sí i tí èèyàn ò bá tètè yàrá fún Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu mi tí ìdílé náà ní láti máa ṣọ́ra fún nípa ikọ́ àti ìṣó? láti máa mí
reference:
Ìyàwó kan rí i pé ọkọ rẹ̀ ń wúkọ́ gan-an nígbà tí wọ́n bá jí ní orí ibùsùn. Ikọ́ náà máa ń bẹ̀rẹ̀ lójijì, ó sì máa ń gba àkókò kí ó tó dáwọ́ dúró. Bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ó tún ń rí i pé ọkọ rẹ̀ ń tiraka láti mí dáadáa. Nígbà tí ó bá rìn jìnnà díẹ̀ tàbí gùn àtẹ̀gùn, ó máa ń dúró láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà, ó tún máa ń rẹ̀ kíákíá.
Ní ọjọ́ kan, lẹ́yìn tí ọkọ rẹ̀ gba àkókò pípẹ́ láti wúkọ́ àti láti gba ẹ̀mí rẹ̀ padà, inú ìyàwó náà bàjẹ́. Ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í rò pé bóyá àrùn kan wà tí ń fa gbogbo àwọn nǹkan wọ̀nyí. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, ó bá ọkọ rẹ̀ sọ̀rọ̀ pé kí wọ́n lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn, kí wọ́n lè rí dókítà, kí wọ́n lè mọ ohun tí ń ṣẹlẹ̀ gan-an.
Ìbéèrè ni pé kí ni ó lè fà kí ikọ́ ní agbára tó bẹ́ẹ̀, kí ara ẹni máa rẹ̀ ní gbogbo ìgbà, kí ènìyàn tún ní ìṣòro mímí dáadáa nígbà gbogbo tí ikọ́ bá ń wáyé? Ṣé ìṣòro yìí lè ní ṣe pẹ̀lú àrùn ẹdọforo tàbí àrùn ọkàn nìkan? Kí ni àwọn ohun tí ó lè mú ikú wá, kí ó sì jẹ́ kí ènìyàn máa tiraka láti mí, tí ó sì lewu débi pé ènìyàn gbọ́dọ̀ tètè lọ ṣàyẹ̀wò?
Kí ni àwọn àmi ewu mímí tí ìdílé gbọ́dọ̀ máa ṣọ́ra fún nípa ikọ́ àti ìṣòro mímí?
model_answer:
A strong cough every morning with breathlessness on walking or climbing stairs is commonly seen in chronic bronchitis/COPD, especially in smokers or people exposed to cooking smoke, dust, or fumes.  
Other important causes include asthma, tuberculosis, pneumonia, heart failure, post-nasal drip, or acid reflux, so it is not only “lung disease”; heart disease can also cause cough and shortness of breath.  
He should be examined at a hospital for chest assessment, oxygen level, sputum testing for TB, chest X-ray, and possibly lung function tests.  
Danger signs needing urgent care include breathlessness at rest, blue lips, chest pain, coughing blood, high fever, night sweats, weight loss, confusion/fainting, swollen legs, or inability to speak full sentences.  
If he smokes, stopping smoking and avoiding smoke/dust exposure is very important while awaiting medical review.

question: Ọ̀kan lára àwọn olóyún wa la rí ní àfẹ̀mọjúmọ̀ yìí pẹ̀lú ọkọ̀ wọn, wọ́n sọ wípé àwọn ní ìrora tí ó lágbára ni inú àwọn tí ẹ̀yin sì ń rú àwọn tí kò sì tí tó ọjọ́ ìbí àwọn abìnrin wabìnrin pé oyún oṣù mélòó ni wọ́n ní tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún oṣù mẹ́fà àti ọjọ́ díẹ̀ a tún wá bẹ̀ wípé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ àbí ohun ò ń fi wọ́n sì sọ pé àwọn ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ nígbà náà ni abo arabìnrin. wí pé njẹ wọn rí omi àbí ẹ̀jẹ̀ san sọ wípé àmúrí omi amọ sì rí ẹ̀jẹ̀ àtúnwá bèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ọmọkeló ní oyún ti wọn ni wọn oyún eleke lo ni oyún tí ó wà nínú tó ń sọ wípé oyún alákọ́èrè wa fún dókítà wa ní wípé mi lè jẹ́ lè tọ́ka sí ààmí ìrọ̀bí àbí àmì wípé oyún bájìn mìíràn ǹjẹ́ a lè sọ? arábìnrin yẹn lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò fọ́tò inú, ilé ìta ń pè ní san láti mú nǹkan tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀.
reference: Ọ̀kan lára àwọn olóyún wa la rí ní àfẹ̀mojúmọ yìí pẹ̀lú ọkọ wọn, wọ́n sọ wípé àwọn ní ìrora tí ó lágbára ní inú àwọn tí ẹ̀yìn sì ń ro àwọn, tí kò sì tíì tó ọjọ́ ìbí àwọn. A béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí pé oyún oṣù mélòó ni wọ́n ní, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún oṣù mẹ́fà àti ọjọ́ díẹ̀. A tún wá béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí pé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ àbí ó mú wọn, ó ń fi wọ́n sílẹ̀, wọ́n sì ní àwọn ní ìrora náà lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́. Nígbà náà ni a béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ǹjẹ́ wọ́n rí omi àbí rí ẹ̀jẹ̀, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé àwọn rí omi àti ẹ̀jẹ̀. A tún wá béèrè lọ́wọ́ arábìnrin yìí wípé ọmọ ẹlẹ́kẹlo, oyún ẹlẹ́kẹlo ni oyún tí ó wà nínú wọn, tí wọ́n sì sọ pé oyún àlá kọ kọ́. Ìbéèrè wa fún dókítà wa ni pé ǹjẹ́ àmì yìí lè tọ́ka sí àmì ìrọbí àbí àmì wípé oyún bàjẹ́ àbí àmì míràn? Ǹjẹ́ a lè sọ wípé kí arábìnrin yìí lọ ṣe àyẹ̀wò fọ́tò inú rẹ̀ tí a ń pè ní <codeswitch> <English> scan láti mọ nǹkan tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀?
model_answer:
Yes, this is an obstetric emergency: at about 6 months pregnancy, severe abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding or watery discharge may indicate preterm labour, premature rupture of membranes, placental abruption, or late miscarriage.  
She should be sent immediately to a hospital with maternity/emergency obstetric care; do not manage her at home or delay for routine ultrasound.  
Assessment should include vital signs, abdominal and speculum examination, fetal heartbeat, ultrasound, and tests for bleeding, infection, and blood group/Rhesus status.  
If the baby is viable, treatment may include steroids for the baby’s lungs, magnesium sulfate, antibiotics if membranes have ruptured, and careful decision on whether to stop labour or deliver depending on mother and baby’s condition.  
Heavy bleeding, severe constant pain, fever, fainting, or reduced fetal movement are danger signs requiring urgent action.

question: Dókítà ìyẹ ọmọkùnrin tó ń gbé ní ilé wa ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ṣe àkíyèsí pé ọmọ rẹ̀ kò mọ ọmú dáadáa ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá gbìyànjú láti fún ní ọmọ náà máa mú díẹ̀ lẹ́yìn náà ó máa dáwọ́ dúró bí ẹni pé ó rẹ́ ọmọ náà tóbi pé ọmọ náà ò ní agbára láti mu ọmú ó sì máa ń làágùn púpọ̀ lórí àti ní ojú rẹ̀ kì í ṣe èyí. nìkan èmi rẹ̀ ó yí padà o máa ń dàbí pé ó ń mi lọ sókè o ń mí lọ sísàlẹ̀ bí ẹni tó ń tiraka láti mí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ ìyá ọmọ náà túbọ̀ ń bẹ̀rù ó ń wò bóyá torí pé ọmọ náà ò jẹ́ ohun tó ni àbí bóyá ó ní ìṣòro kan nípa èyí àti bó ṣe ń láàgùn nítorí náà ó pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn láti rí dókítà fún. wò ọmọ náà ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fàá kí ọmọ máa ń ní ìṣòro láti mu ọmú dáadáa náà ṣe mí jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera kankan tí òbí ọmọ náà ní kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún ló lè fa? Bí ọmọdé máa làágùn nígbà tó bá ń mu omú.
reference:
Dokita, iya ọmọ kan tó ń gbé ní ilé wa, ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ń ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ rẹ kò mu ọmú dáadáa. Ní gbogbo ìgbà tí ó bá gbìyànjú láti fún un ní ọmú, ọmọ náà máa mu díẹ̀, lẹ́yìn náà ó máa dáwọ́ dúró bí ẹni pé ó rẹ̀ẹ́. Ìyá ọmọ náà tún rí pé ọmọ náà kò ní agbára láti mu ọmú, ó sì máa ń làágùn púpọ̀ lórí àti ní ojú rẹ̀. Kì í ṣe èyí nìkan, èémí rẹ̀ ó yí padà, ó máa ń dàbí pé ó ń mí lọ sókè, ó ń mí lọ sísàlẹ̀, bí ẹni tó ń tiraka láti mí. Bí ọjọ́ ṣe ń lọ, ìyá ọmọ náà ń túbọ̀ ń bẹ̀rù, ó ń wo bóyá torí pé ọmọ náà kò jẹun tó ni, àbí bóyá ó ní ìṣòro kan nípa èémí àti bóyá ṣe ń làágùn. Nítorí náà, ó pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Láti rí dókítà fún àyẹ̀wò ọmọ náà. Ìbéèrè mi ni wípé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ máa ní ìṣòro láti mu ọmú dáadáa? Ṣé bí ọmọ náà ṣe ń mí jẹ́ àmì ìṣòro ìlera kankan? Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tí òbí ọmọ náà ní kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún? Kí ló lè fa kí ọmọ kékeré máa làágùn nígbà tí ó bá ń mu ọmú?
English Translation
model_answer:
Sweating and tiring during breastfeeding, especially with fast or laboured breathing, is a warning sign and can be due to congenital heart disease causing heart failure in the baby.  
Other possible causes include pneumonia or other chest infection, severe anaemia, prematurity/low birth weight, poor latch, or metabolic problems, but the combination of sweating, breathlessness and poor feeding needs urgent medical assessment.  
Parents should watch for bluish lips or tongue, breathing faster than normal, chest indrawing, poor weight gain, swelling, fever, extreme sleepiness, or passing little urine.  
The baby should be taken to a hospital promptly for examination, oxygen level check, weight assessment, chest/heart evaluation, and possibly echocardiography.  
Until reviewed, feed in small frequent amounts and keep the baby upright, but do not delay seeking care.

question: ọmọ kan yóò ṣàkíyèsí fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ báyìí ọmọ yẹn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní wúkọ́ láì dáwọ́ dúró ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀ kúrò pé òtútù lóko sọmọ náà láyà pé ó máa lọ ṣùgbọ́n ikọ́ náà kò dínkù ní gbogbo alẹ́ ọmọ náà máa jí nílòji nítorí ikọ́ nígbà mi ó máa ń wù wá bẹ́ẹ̀ ni pé ó ṣò. Gbogbo fún láti lè mí dáadáa máa gbé sókè ó sì máa gbọ́ bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́ nígbà tó bá mú èyí ń mu kí ọmọ náà máa lè sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́ ní ọjọ́ kan lẹ́yìn alẹ́ tí ọmọ náà tó wúkọ́ gan tó sì tiraka láti lè mí dáadáa ìyá rẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ sí. Ilé ìwòsàn ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa iko náà àti ìṣòro tó fi ń tó fa láti mí dáadáa àti bí ó ṣe lè rán ọmọ náà lọ́wọ́ béèrè mi ni pé kí ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ máa wuko gan kò sì ní ìṣòro láti lè mí dáadáa pàápàá ní alẹ́ kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra? Fún nígbà tí ọmọ náà bá ń wúkọ́ àwọn nǹkan wo ló yẹ kí wọ́n yàgò fún láti dènà ikọ yìí?
reference:
Ìyá ọmọ kan ló ṣàkíyèsí wípé fún ọjọ́ díẹ̀ báyìí, pé ọmọ òun bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í wúkọ láì dáwọ́ dúró. Ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀, ó rò pé òtútù ló kọ ọmọ náà láyà, pé ó máa lọ. Ṣùgbọ́n ikọ́ náà kò dínkù. Ní gbogbo alẹ́, ọmọ náà máa jí lójijì nítorí ikọ́. Nígbà míì, ó máa ń wíwá bí ẹni pé ó ṣòro fún un láti mí dáadáa. Ìyá rẹ̀ máa gbé e sókè, ó sì máa gbọ́ bí àyà rẹ̀ ṣe ń ṣiṣẹ́ nígbà tí ó bá ń mí. Èyí mú kí ọmọ náà má lè sùn dáadáa ní alẹ́.
Ní ọjọ́ kan, lẹ́yìn alẹ́ tí ọmọ náà ti wúkọ gan-an tí ó sì tiraka láti mí dáadáa, ìyá rẹ̀ pinnu láti lọ sí ilé ìwòsàn. Ó fẹ́ mọ ohun tó fa ikọ́ náà àti ìṣòro tó fa láti má lè mí dáadáa, àti bí ó ṣe lè ràn án lọ́wọ́.
Ìbéèrè mi ni pé kí ló lè fa kí ọmọ máa wúkọ gan, kí ó sì ní ìṣòro láti mí dáadáa pàápàá ní alẹ́? Kí ni àwọn àmì ewu tí ó yẹ kí wọ́n máa ṣọ́ra fún nígbà tí ọmọ náà bá ń wúkọ? Àwọn nǹkan wo ló yẹ kí wọ́n yàgò fún láti dènà ikọ́ yìí?
model_answer:
A child with persistent cough worse at night plus wheezing or “chest working hard” may have asthma/reactive airway disease triggered by a viral cold, dust or smoke, but pneumonia, bronchiolitis, whooping cough, TB, or an inhaled foreign body must also be considered.  
Because the child is struggling to breathe, they should be examined urgently at a hospital for respiratory rate, oxygen level, chest signs, and treatment such as inhaled salbutamol/nebulization, oxygen, or antibiotics only if indicated.  
Danger signs are fast breathing, chest indrawing, noisy breathing/stridor, blue lips, inability to drink or breastfeed, extreme weakness/drowsiness, convulsions, persistent high fever, vomiting everything, or cough lasting more than 2 weeks with weight loss/night sweats.  
To reduce attacks, avoid cigarette smoke, cooking smoke/charcoal or kerosene fumes, dust, strong perfumes/insecticides, cold air, mold, and known triggers such as pets or certain foods if clearly linked.  
Do not give adult medicines, leftover antibiotics, or sedating cough mixtures; keep the child upright, offer fluids, and follow the clinician’s plan including inhaler technique if asthma is diagnosed.

question: Ọmọ mi ẹni ọdún mẹ́sàn ni mo gbé wá sí ilé ìwòsàn ní ọ̀sán yìí mo ná ọmọ náà níṣẹ́ láti ra nǹkan fún mi ní ìgboro ṣùgbọ́n a já bu ọmọ náà jẹ nígbà tí wọ́n mú ọmọ náà délé tí wọ́n sì ṣàlàyé fún mi tó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ọmọ náà mo wo ojú egbò tí ajá ti bu ọmọ náà jẹ mo rí pé ojú egbò náà pọ́n ó sì ti wú a ṣe ìwádìí ládùgbò láti mor tó ọmọ náà jẹ́ olówó ajá náà sì sọ wípé àwọn kò gba abere fún ajá náà rí pé lẹ́yìn kí ó jáde kó ṣeré kó sì padà wọlé, wọ́n ní àwọn ogbà ìtọ́jú kankan fún ajá náà rì ni ẹ̀rù ṣe bà mí láti gbé ọmọ náà wá sí ilé ìwòsàn kó má jẹ́ wípé ajá tó bu ọmọ náà jẹ́ ó jẹ́ ajá digbolugi Kí ló ṣeéṣe kó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ọmọ tí a já bùjẹ? Kí ló ṣeéṣe kí ó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ojú egbò tí ó ń pọ́n tí ó sì ń wú? N ó ṣe kí ẹran ipá tí ẹ ti wọnú egbò yìí ó ṣe kí ọmọ náà kó kí nǹkan kó ṣe ọmọ. Ọmọ náà látàrí ọmọ tí a já wo ni mo lè ṣe láti má jẹ́ kí ẹran ipa wọnú egbò yìí awọn abẹ́rẹ́ wo àwọn oògùn a lè fi tọ́jú ọmọdé yìí láti jẹ́ kó ní ìtọ́jú tó péye. Àwọn ohun wo ni a tún lè ṣe tàbí ayewo lale ṣe láti tọju oju egbo ti a ja ti ọmọde.
reference:
Ọmọ mi ẹni ọdun mẹsan ni mo gbe wa si ile-iwosan ni ọsan yi. Mo ran ọmọ naa ni iṣẹ lati ra nkan fun mi ni igboro, ṣugbọn aja bu ọmọ naa jẹ. Nigba ti wọn mu ọmọ naa dele, ti wọn si ṣalaye fun mi ohun to ṣẹlẹ si ọmọ naa, mo wo oju egbo ti aja ti bu ọmọ naa jẹ, mo ri pe oju egbo naa pọn, o si ti wú. A ṣe iwadi ni adugbo lati mọ irú aja to bu ọmọ naa jẹ, olowo aja naa si sọ wipe awọn kò gba abẹrẹ fun aja naa rí, wipe lẹyin ki o jade, ko ṣere, ko si pada wọle. Wọn ni awọn o gba itọju kankan fun aja naa rí. Idi eyi ni ẹru ṣe bami lati gbe ọmọ naa wa si ile-iwosan, ko ma jẹ wipe aja to bu ọmọ naa jẹ, o jẹ aja digbolugi. Ki lo ṣeṣe ko ṣẹlẹ si ọmọ ti aja bu jẹ yi? Ki lo ṣeṣe ko ṣẹlẹ si oju egbo ti o n pọn, ti o si n wú? N jẹ o ṣeṣe ki ẹran ipa ti ẹ ti wọnu egbo yi? N jẹ o ṣeṣe ki ọmọ naa... ki nkan ko ṣe ọmọ naa latari ọmọ ti aja bu jẹ? Ẹ jọọ...
Awọn wo ni mo le ṣe lati ma jẹ ki ẹran ipa wọnu egbo yi? Awọn abẹrẹ wo, awọn ogun wo ni a le fi tọju ọmọde yi lati jẹ ko ni itọju to peye? Awọn wo ni a tun le ṣe tabi ayẹwo wo la le ṣe lati tọju oju egbo ti aja ti bu ọmọde yi jẹ?
model_answer:
A bite from an unvaccinated dog is high risk for rabies and wound infection; rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so treatment must start immediately, without waiting to see if the dog becomes sick.  
The red, swollen wound suggests inflammation or cellulitis from bacteria in the dog’s mouth, and the child also needs tetanus protection.  
Wash the wound thoroughly with running water and soap for at least 15 minutes, apply povidone-iodine/chlorhexidine, remove dead tissue/foreign material, and avoid tight primary stitching unless a clinician decides it is necessary.  
Give rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, and 14, plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound if this is a deep/transdermal bite or saliva entered broken skin.  
The child should also receive tetanus vaccine/immune globulin as indicated, antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5–7 days, pain relief, and assessment for pus, abscess, tendon/nerve injury, fracture or foreign body, with X-ray/culture if needed.

question: Alágbà tó ṣàkíyèsí wípé ọmọ náà ń wúkọ́ gidigidi débi pé ó ń ta gì pé ọmọ náà gbìyànjú tiraka láti mí dáradára ni ó lè fa kí ọmọ kí ó máa wúkó àtarìbi wí pé kò lè mí dáadáa tó ń tiraka láti mi irú ni a lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà ìtọ́jú wo ni a lè fún Bákan náà irú ìmọ̀ràn wo ni a lè gba ìyá ọ lágbà ìtọ́jú ọmọdé náà?
reference: Alágbàtọ́ ọmọ kan ṣàkíyèsí pé ọmọ náà wúkọ́ gidigidi, dé bi pé òun tàgìrì àti wí pé ọmọ náà gbìyànjú tiraka láti mí dáradára ni. Kí ó le fa kí ọmọ kí ó máa n wúkọ́ àwú tagìrì, débi wípé kò le mí dáadáa, tó tiraka láti mí? Irú àyẹ̀wò wo la lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà? Irú ìtọ́jú wo la lè fún? Bákan náà irú àmọ̀rà wo la lè gba Alágbàtọ́ ọmọ náà?
model_answer:
Severe cough with struggling to breathe in a child can be caused by pneumonia, asthma/bronchiolitis, croup, whooping cough, or choking/foreign body aspiration, and it is a medical emergency if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, blue lips, inability to feed, lethargy, or noisy breathing.  
The child should be taken immediately to the nearest hospital/clinic for assessment of oxygen level, chest examination, and treatment such as oxygen, nebulized salbutamol if wheezing, antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected, steroids for croup/asthma, or urgent removal of a foreign body if choking is suspected.  
Do not give cough syrups, sedatives, antibiotics, or herbal mixtures without a clinician’s prescription, as they may delay proper treatment or harm the child.  
While going to hospital, keep the child sitting upright, loosen tight clothing, keep the airway clear, and continue breastfeeding/small fluids only if the child can swallow safely.  
Advise the mother to avoid smoke and dust exposure, complete immunizations, ensure good nutrition, and seek care early whenever cough is associated with fever, fast breathing, chest indrawing, poor feeding, or worsening symptoms.

question: Arabinrin ọmọ ogbon odun lo bimọ bi iṣẹju merinlelogbon seyin a sọ pe bi ṣe rọrun nigba ti arabinrin yii bi ọmọ rẹ omo naa n sun ju o nira fun gan lati ke ko si ṣe daada ọmọ naa ko sunkun pupọ lẹsẹkẹsẹ nigbati a bi tan o si dabi ẹni pe o nira fun lati ji Àwọ̀ ara rẹ̀ dá bí ẹni pé ó fẹ́ sán kò gbé apá rẹ̀ àti ẹsẹ̀ rẹ̀ dáadáa bó ṣe yẹ kó gbún lè jẹun torí wípé ó ń sùn jù kò sì lè fa ọmú dáadáa ìyá ọmọ náà ṣe àníyàn wípé àwọn ọmọ òun tó bí tẹ́lẹ̀ kété tí òun bá bí wọn tán, wọ́n máa ń sunkún lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ yìí? Àwọn àyẹ̀wò wo ni a lè ṣe lórí ọmọ náà àti wípé ìgbésẹ̀ ìpajárì wo ni a gbọ́dọ̀ gbé lórí ọmọ náà kò ké dáadáa bó ṣe yẹ kó sunkún fá ọmú dáadáa náà kí la lè ṣe lórí ọmọ náà kékeré ni ọmọ tó ṣẹ̀bi ni ọmọ náà kí la lè ṣe fún ọmọ náà?
reference:
Arábìnrin kan, ẹni ọdún ọgbọ̀n, ló bímọ ní ìṣẹ́jú díẹ̀ sẹ́yìn. A sọ pé ìbímọ náà lọ dáadáa. Ṣùgbọ́n láti ìgbà tí a bí ọmọ náà, ọmọ náà ń ṣòro gan-an. Kò ń sunkún dáadáa, kò sì ń dáhùn bí ọmọ tuntun ṣe yẹ.
Lẹ́yìn ìbí, ọmọ náà kò súnkún dáadáa, ó sì dà bí ẹni pé ó ní ìṣòro láti jí. Ara rẹ̀ dá bí ẹni pé kò rọrùn, ọwọ́ àti ẹsẹ̀ rẹ̀ kò ń rìn dáadáa bí ó ṣe yẹ. Kò tún lè jẹun dáadáa, ó sì ń ṣòro fún un láti fà ọmú.
Ìyá ọmọ náà ṣe àníyàn torí pé àwọn ọmọ rẹ̀ tó ti bí tẹ́lẹ̀ máa ń sunkún lẹ́sẹ̀kẹsẹ̀ lẹ́yìn ìbí. Kí ni ó lè fà ìṣòro yìí? Àwọn àyẹ̀wò wo ni a lè ṣe lórí ọmọ náà, àti kí ni ìgbésẹ̀ pajawiri tí a lè gbé? Kí ni a lè ṣe fún ọmọ kékeré yìí?
model_answer:
This baby has danger signs of neonatal depression/birth asphyxia and must be managed as an emergency, not just allowed to sleep.  
Immediately dry and keep the baby warm, position the head, clear the airway only if blocked, stimulate gently, check breathing and heart rate, and start bag-mask ventilation if not breathing well or heart rate is below 100/min; add oxygen if available and give chest compressions if heart rate remains below 60/min after effective ventilation.  
Assess Apgar score, temperature, weight/gestational age, oxygen saturation, heart rate, respiratory effort, tone, colour, and check blood glucose urgently; if glucose is low or baby cannot suck, give IV 10% dextrose according to protocol.  
Do not force breastfeeding until stable; give expressed breast milk by cup/tube only when breathing is safe, and consider IV fluids, antibiotics if infection risk, and monitoring for seizures or hypoxic brain injury.  
The baby should be referred/admitted urgently to a newborn unit or hospital with neonatal resuscitation and oxygen support.

Bluish lips/mouth in a newborn with difficulty breathing, especially during breastfeeding, is a danger sign called cyanosis and needs urgent hospital care immediately.

If any suicide risk is present, do not leave her alone—remove dangerous objects/medicines and take her immediately to an emergency unit or contact local emergency/mental health services.

This sounds like secondary postpartum haemorrhage, a dangerous bleeding occurring days after delivery, most commonly due to retained placental tissue, infection of the womb, poor uterine contraction, or genital tract tears.  
She should be treated as an emergency: check vital signs, establish two large IV lines, give IV fluids, take blood for grouping/crossmatch, and transfuse if needed.  
To stop the bleeding, give uterotonics such as oxytocin or misoprostol, massage the uterus, examine for retained products or tears, evacuate/repair if present, and give broad-spectrum antibiotics if infection is suspected.

Blue lips or tongue in a newborn during feeding means low oxygen and is an emergency; it can be caused by serious heart defects, lung infection/pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration of milk, airway blockage, prematurity-related apnea, or other breathing/neurological problems.  
Difficulty breathing, stopping breathing, limpness, poor feeding, fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, fever or low temperature, repeated vomiting, convulsions, unusual sleepiness, or worsening blue/grey colour are danger signs requiring urgent hospital care.  
Yes, congenital heart disease and lung disease can both cause cyanosis and breathlessness, especially when the baby is feeding because feeding increases oxygen demand.  
If it happens, stop feeding immediately, place the baby on the back or side with the head in a neutral position, gently clear visible milk/mucus from the mouth/nose, stimulate by rubbing the back/feet, keep the baby warm, and go to the emergency unit immediately.  
If the baby is not breathing or has no movement, start infant CPR if trained and call for urgent medical help; do not give herbal mixtures, water, or force more feeding.

A newborn who is very sleepy, not crying well, breathing poorly, and feels cold has danger signs and may have birth asphyxia, prematurity/low birth weight, hypothermia, low blood sugar, infection/sepsis, or effects of drugs given to the mother during labour.  
This baby needs immediate neonatal care in the hospital: keep warm with skin-to-skin/Kangaroo care or incubator, check temperature, blood sugar and oxygen level, clear the airway, stimulate, give oxygen/CPAP or resuscitation if needed, and start antibiotics if infection is suspected.  
Do not take such a baby home until breathing, temperature, feeding, and blood sugar are stable and a clinician has assessed the baby.  
At home, give only breast milk—direct breastfeeding if the baby can suck, or expressed breast milk by cup/spoon or feeding tube if advised; feed frequently, keep the baby warm, and attend follow-up/immunization visits.  
Do not give water, herbal mixtures, glucose water, honey, alcohol, gripe water, or unprescribed medicines, and return urgently if the baby is cold/hot, not feeding, breathing fast or with pauses, blue, convulsing, vomiting repeatedly, or becoming more sleepy.
